source_record_provenance.record_title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text empirically analyzes linguistic representations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by measuring activation differences across linguistic minimal pairs and computing linguistic similarity (∆z = z+ − z−; sim(∆z1, ∆z2) via cosine similarity).
The study employs a large-scale experimental setup with 100+ LLMs across three languages and 150k linguistic minimal pairs, using activation-based analysis.
The work uses 104 LLMs from Huggingface (transformer-based models) and evaluates them on linguistic minimal pairs from BLiMP (English), SLING (Chinese), and RuBLiMP (Russian).

The research targets syntactic phenomena (e.g., binding, subject–verb agreement, NPI licensing) through linguistic minimal pairs datasets, and reports empirical measurements of linguistic similarity across models.

Stage 2 evidence includes an empirical analysis of alignment across LLMs (e.g., mutual k-nearest neighbors) and language-specific patterns (English showing higher alignment; multilingual/bilingual clustering in Chinese).
evidence_highlights: Activations: ∆z = z+ − z− and linguistic similarity sim(∆z1, ∆z2) are computed to isolate the representation of specific linguistic phenomena.
Data and models: 150k minimal pairs across BLiMP, SLING, RuBLiMP; 104 LLMs from Huggingface (transformer-based) evaluated.
Methodology: Activation differences are stored and analyzed across five layers, with cosine similarity used for comparisons.
Results: English BLiMP shows highest LLM alignment scores (average ~0.471), Chinese SLING ~0.414, Russian RuBLiMP ~0.139.
Cross-language findings: linguistic phenomena tend to cluster by language in multilingual LLMs, with cross-language attractions observed between English and Chinese phenomena.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: Full-text evidence demonstrates a clear, empirical analysis of syntactic representations in Transformer-based LLMs via linguistic minimal pairs, using large-scale multi-language data and activation-based similarity metrics. There are explicit inclusion signals (syntactic phenomena analysis, empirical evaluation across many LLMs, datasets BLiMP/SLING/RuBLiMP) and no explicit exclusion triggers (no focus on non-transformer architectures or non-empirical work). Therefore, Stage 2 criteria are strongly satisfied and the paper should be included.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The paper probes for morphosyntactic properties in word representations, i.e., intrinsic morphosyntactic probing (Section 3.3).
It uses a decomposable probabilistic probe based on a Gaussian p(h|v) to examine which subset of dimensions carries morphosyntactic information (Sections 3.1–3.3).
The study experiments on 36 languages from UD treebanks mapped to UniMorph, using both BERT (Transformer-based LM) and fastText word embeddings (Section 5).
It reports empirical metrics (LBA, LBMI/LBNMI) and provides quantitative evaluation across dimensions and languages (Sections 4, 6; Fig. 2).
Findings show morphosyntactic information is more focal in fastText and more dispersed in BERT, with dimensionality requirements around 10 vs 35 respectively (Section 6).
evidence_highlights: Decomposable Gaussian probe enabling constant-time evaluation for subsets of dimensions (Gaussian–inverse-Wishart framework) (Sections 3.1–3.4).
Empirical evaluation across 36 languages with BERT and fastText; uses UD→UniMorph mapping; reports LBA and MI-based metrics (Sections 5–6).
FastText tends to encode morphosyntactic properties using fewer dimensions than BERT (≈10 vs ≈35) (Figure 2).
LBMI/LBNMI as robust metrics for cross-language, cross-attribute comparison (Section 4.2).
The approach is framed as intrinsic probing of morphosyntax rather than extrinsic tasks (Sections 2–3).
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it centers on Transformer-based language models (BERT) and empirically analyzes morphosyntactic structure via an intrinsic, decomposable probing framework; it provides a concrete method (Gaussian probe) with a Bayesian treatment and reports extensive empirical evaluation across multiple languages, aligning with the stipulated Stage 2 requirements. title: Deep Clustering of Text Representations for Supervision-Free Probing of Syntax

source_record_provenance.record_title: Deep Clustering of Text Representations for Supervision-Free Probing of Syntax

satisfied_inclusion_points: The abstract discusses unsupervised model interpretation and induction of syntax from multilingual text representations.
It explicitly includes POSI and CoLab as notions of syntax to evaluate.
It mentions evaluation/claims of syntax knowledge in multilingual BERT (mBERT) and E-BERT.
It frames the approach as a supervision-free probe for syntax.
It reports competitive performance on POSI and CoLab across languages, including cross-language results.
evidence_highlights: We explore deep clustering of multilingual text representations for unsupervised model interpretation and induction of syntax.
We consider two notions of syntax: Part of Speech Induction (POSI) and Constituency Labelling (CoLab) in this work.
Interestingly, we find that Multilingual BERT (mBERT) contains surprising amount of syntactic knowledge of English; possibly even as much as English BERT (E-BERT).
Our model can be used as a supervision-free probe which is arguably a less-biased way of probing.
We validate the efficacy of our probe by demonstrating its capabilities as a unsupervised syntax induction technique.
We report competitive performance of our probe on 45-tag English POSI, state-of-the-art performance on 12-tag POSI across 10 languages, and competitive results on CoLab.
We also perform zero-shot syntax induction on resource impoverished languages and report strong results.
stage1_review.decision_rationale: Stage 1 evidence clearly supports that the paper analyzes syntactic knowledge in transformer-based language models via empirical probing and reports cross-linguistic results, aligning with the Stage 1 inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria are evident from the title/abstract.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text presents a systematic study of contextualized word representations in ELMo and BERT (Transformer-based LMs), as stated: "We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT."
It empirically analyzes syntactic structure/knowledge via three syntax-related tasks: Part of Speech Tagging (POS), Dependency Label Prediction (DLP), and Dependency Edge Prediction (DEP).
The paper shows that a variety of linguistic features, including structured dependency relationships, are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces.

It demonstrates that these low-dimensional subspaces are causally related to model behavior through ablation experiments (e.g., removing POS-related subspaces affects predictions like subject–verb agreement).
The work reveals hierarchical structure within subspaces (e.g., POS subtask hierarchies) and that these subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than axis-aligned.
evidence_highlights: Abstract states that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces and that these subspaces are causally related to model behavior.
Tasks include POS, DLP, and DEP across representations (ELMo and BERT).
Results show d<10 for POS/DLP and d<21 for DEP, indicating low-dimensional encodings.
Ablation in section 6 demonstrates causal impact on subject–verb agreement.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it analyzes syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based models (BERT) with empirical syntax probing, demonstrates encoding of syntax in low-dimensional subspaces, shows hierarchical structure and distributed representations, and provides causal evidence via ablation that these subspaces influence model behavior.
